title: Florida Citrus Growers Fight to Keep an Industry Alive
full_text:
FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE AND CONSUMER AFFAIRS /
COURTESY PHOTO
Michael Rogers, Ph.D., a professor and the director, was laboring in the Citrus Research & Education Center on the aptly named Experiment Station Road in Lake Alfred one morning recently when Ed English and his nephew Trey English parked their vehicles in a farmyard many miles to the south. They ignored the gray midday drizzle and walked out to hundreds of net-covered young grapefruit trees. Then they took stock of the situation.
The grove appeared to be vibrant and healthy. About 40 acres of two-year-old trees flourished under nets likely to stay on through their third year, designed to protect them when they’re young from a disease called greening.
On a gray November morning, Trey English and his uncle, Ed English, stand among 40 acres of young grapefruit trees they aim to establish in the face of greening.
ROGER WILLIAMS /COURTESY PHOTO
Greening, aka Huanglongbing (HLB) after its century-old Chinese origin, is no joke. In two short decades, the disease reduced the Florida citrus industry by about 95%, according to the USDA. Farmers couldn’t stiff-arm it or work around it, and researchers still haven’t found a cure for the thing itself or created new citrus varieties that could remain unaffected by it, although they may be close.
The year before they first noticed greening in 2005, the Sunshine State’s growers produced the greatest harvest ever recorded in a single 12-month period. From countless miles of citrus groves — their trees flanked roads and blanketed landscapes from the Lake Wales ridge country of central Florida to the flat wet stretches of the southern peninsula — those growers sent almost 250 million boxes to market, at 90 pounds of oranges per box, and 85 pounds per box of grapefruit.
Last year, the statewide harvest was about 14 million boxes, and this year, the USDA and Florida’s agricultural experts estimate a harvest of 10 million boxes. That will be a reduction of almost 96% from 2004, with more than 90% of the acres in citrus operations affected by greening.
Land devoted to citrus amounted to more than 748,500 acres in 2004. Two decades later, in 2024, growers tried to produce viable fruit on about 274,700 acres, according to industry analysts at the University of Florida.
But the larger supporting economy also went away. No more (now just one or two) processing plants. No more roadside stands. No more trucks crowding roads in harvest seasons, their trailers so full of freshly picked oranges that intersections where they had to make turns became pocked with fruit falling off the top and hitting the pavement.
The decades-old English grove on Cemetery Road is now home to promising new grapefruit trees rooted in hope and organic soil.
ROGER WILLIAMS /COURTESY PHOTO
As recently as 2020, in the English Grove, both sides of the one-lane, dead-end Cemetery Road, not quite a mile long, were crowded with hundreds of acres of the family citrus. On spring nights, the fragrance of blossoms could drift for miles across eastern Lee County in Alva, where Trey grew up in a farming family before setting off into a higher education that led to his Ph.D. in computer engineering from Purdue University.
While his father, the late Jim English, and uncles Ed, Joe and Hugh downshifted a lifetime of high-energy effort, Trey returned to support a move forward into what may become the new citrus world — more specialized sales relying on regional markets, with high-quality fruit from trees grown with decades of research and inventive growing methods that successfully tolerate greening.
Such trees would take in nutrients and produce enviable fruit in significant quantities for years, without being suffocated by the disease. Passed or “vectored” by an insect smaller than the head of a pin, the Asian citrus psyllid, a bacterium slowly inhibits the tree’s vascular system, eventually shutting off its ability to take in sufficient water and nutrients through the roots.
In a heartbreaking farming moment repeated across the Florida landscape, the Englishes had to take down every tree along Cemetery Road, stack them in great forlorn piles, burn dead wood and remove the remainder, then introduce organic soil hauled in to infuse part of the old grove where they planned to try again.
Now on the gray November morning in question, the grove is a work of both old art and new science that seems to suggest at least one truth, whether they succeed or not: These citrus farmers are resilient, able to adapt, and willing to try new approaches in the face of massive challenges, rather than sell out to development and walk away with cash, or do something else.
The current situation
Hendry County citrus includes new trees among old ones at great risk of greening.
ROGER WILLIAMS / FLORIDA WEEKLY
So far, there’s no sign of greening in the English grove.
In the larger world of citrus, though, the situation appears dire now in the autumn of 2026, but that’s nothing new.
“The disease has been here since 2005, and we’ve learned so much over the past two decades,” Rogers said.  “All that knowledge, and we’ve developed new approaches to how we grow citrus, so there are tools to help in the short term.”
A CREC employee working the juice analysis process at the Citrus Research and Education Center (CREC) .
TYLER JONES, UF/IFAS / COURTESY PHOTO
But the remaining farmers and growers statewide are struggling to regain at least some of the prominent place they once held in Florida’s character and capacity. Now, they’re near desperate for long-term solutions, they say.
“As for the long-term solutions — the ultimate tools — we’re looking (in lab and field) for a citrus tree resistant to disease,” Rogers explained.
“There are new citrus varieties released by the University of Florida that survive better than old varieties we’ve grown in last 100 years. We have some 10- and 12-year-old groves producing several hundreds of boxes of fruit more than traditional varieties, so there’s promise there.”
And then there’s biotechnology — gene editing.
“That technology didn’t exist 15 years ago,” Rogers noted, “but we’ve identified genes in the plant that play a role in disease, and we can cut those out or turn them off.”
Michael Rogers at the Citrus Research and Education Center (CREC)
TYLER JONES, UF/IFAS / COURTESY PHOTO
Time, therefore, still separates the reality from the long-term solution in ending the greening assault. But not as much time, perhaps, for those who can endure.
“We have a lot of field trials now taking place at UF, and we’re hopeful some will work well,” Rogers said.
“We’re excited about all of that. We have thousands and thousands of trees in the field, and they won’t all work (by tolerating greening enough to produce fruit every year), but if one or two do, that would be a win.”
In getting to this point in the 20-year odyssey of resilience and survival, researchers have helped growers understand how all this works. “We had no idea what we were dealing with, when this first hit us,” remembers Wayne Simmons, a farmer in Hendry County who still maintains about 250 acres of citrus outside of Labelle.
But now everybody knows: the bacterium creates a slow death, putting great stress on the trees and breaking them down over time by “taking out the root system of trees so they can’t pick up water and nutrients effectively,” Rogers explains.
“So the first step is to pick up water and nutrients.”
Hanging on
A majority of one-time citrus growers are out of the business today because they couldn’t wait through 20 or more years for research to catch up with greening.
A mature grove
T. WEEKS, UF/IFAS / COURTESY PHOTO
But not the Englishes, and not Wayne Simmons, who are still standing.
“You don’t know the commitment it takes to stay in the citrus business now,” he said. “It’s not for the faint of heart. It’s so intense, so hands on, you have to really put out, be out there every day checking to see what the trees look like — one day a grove will look good and the next day it looks totally different.”
Simmons grew up on a farm in central Florida and moved south where there was more land and more room to grow. First, though, he earned a degree in agriculture from the University of Florida. Like the Englishes, he knows what he’s doing.
“A layman couldn’t tell, but we’ve had to be better managers of fertilizer, of water, of chemicals — and all these things affect the bottom line, as well,” he said.
In the early days of greening, Simmons acknowledged, “we tried to spray our way out of it.”
That the approach failed hasn’t dissuaded him from this conviction: “Florida is made to grow liquid sunshine. We’re meant to grow oranges. And it used to be, anybody could grow oranges in Florida. It’s why some winter visitors come down — they can plant an orange tree in their yard.”
Not anymore, not with certainty.
Nevertheless, some intrepid growers refuse to give up.
The biggest challenges
When asked what the two biggest challenges facing the remaining citrus growers in Florida might be, they’ll all name “greening.” A worldwide disease, it has nevertheless devastated Florida’s industry.
But they’ll also generally point to the economy and their weakened capacity to sell fruit at prices that allow them to do more than just break even, or worse.
Sights you don’t see regularly on the roads anymore.
ROGER WILLIAMS / FLORIDA WEEKLY
The old standards growers and other farmers face — drought, freezes and hurricanes — don’t even make the top of the list of hardest challenges anymore.
“We have two problems now,” Ed English said, speaking from the experience of more than eight decades: “Production, and marketing.”
With his brothers Hugh, Jim and Joe, he grew up in a family that produced fruit and raised cows at a time when production and marketing may not have been big problems or at least not the same ones. He took some time as a young man to get a degree in agriculture focusing on citrus from the Florida Southern College, and carried on when the English family had hundreds, if not more, acres of citrus in Southwest Florida.
Now Ed is 87, a man whose elders — including a father who had come from a time of no electricity or running water but seen Neil Armstrong step onto the moon on live television — understood the challenges in different terms.
“I asked my father what the biggest change he’d seen in his life had been,” Ed remembered, “and what do you think he said?”
Maybe the answer was men landing on the moon. Cars? Jets? Vaccines?
None of the above.
“Good food,’ he told me. When he was young, they didn’t even have refrigeration,” Ed said.
In those days, citrus consumption in juice or fruit was often fresh and local, and if it was shipped out, it might first go by train to American cities. Citrus didn’t require immediate and consistent refrigeration, so it could be exported well.
But the economics and distribution of such food began to change.
Trey grew up like Ed, in the same groves on the same fields, but in a time with electricity and therefore easy refrigeration, highways, trucks and airplanes. And a lot more people. Like his uncle Ed and his brothers, he went off to college, too. But unlike that generation, he proceeded on through graduate school, earning a Ph.D. in computer engineering.
Then he came back, working as a consultant in that field, but taking up farming again, too.  In 2022 and ‘23, when the Englishes had to clear hundreds of acres of citrus damaged or killed by greening, they decided to invest the soil on about 40 acres with nourishing organic materials. Then in 2024 they planted new young grapefruit trees.
Now Trey English — with other remaining growers and the University of Florida’s researchers in Lake Alfred all looking for ways to defeat greening in the long term — is the hope of the citrus industry.
They could probably sell their land to developers and make a tidy profit, but they refuse to quit.
Nevertheless, money matters.
“The number 2 worry behind greening is economic,” Trey said.
“Florida’s citrus industry is collapsing. In a single generation we’ve gone to absolute bust. But citrus worldwide is growing. It’s booming in China, and it’s not because they don’t have greening. Greening comes from China and India.
Trees with fruit
T. WEEKS, UF/IFAS / COURTESY PHOTO
“And they have greening in Brazil and Mexico. But (all those places) have a geographic diversity Florida doesn’t.”
They can plant citrus higher and drier where the psyllid doesn’t do well, for example. They can simply move to another area or region. And they can rely on so-called mom-and-pop operations where they do all the labor (that’s a Chinese approach, not designed for an international market, say, the American farmers).
Any crop Florida’s farmers harvest has to balance the cost of now more elaborate maintenance and growing requirements for citrus.
Meanwhile, even if a citrus that seemed abundantly available again in an industry that seemed impregnable were to come back as robustly as it existed once upon a time, the world has changed around it.
Processing plants are all but gone, a labor force is weakened and thin, and the market may have changed.
Ed English, with the widest experience of any grower, a man as pragmatic and adaptable as any, sees great opportunity in it all — a great market.
He has confidence in the science and in growers' ability to adjust, given time and some resources, he says. As for the market?
“In 1940 when I was born, there were about 15,000 people in Lee County. (site census figures for the county and for Florida). Now there are almost 900,000,” he said.
“That’s a market. Fresh and local. They’ll need to figure out how to reach it.”
The English grove that could do that — that he spent his life carrying on so he could share the life, work and the fruit, passing such a life to his nephew — stands off a road that dead-ends in a cemetery for a seeming reason. The cemetery itself is populated by a number of people Ed and Trey English knew, including relatives who taught them things they still use to grow citrus, and somehow to carry on.
Is citrus ever going to come back and produce the way it once did in Florida?
“I don’t think it will,” said Ed English.
“Seems unlikely,” said Trey.
And that may not matter now.
Joy is part of what the living generation of citrus farmers may have learned from once upon a time — part of what the old-timers taught them to harvest with their fruit, perhaps. That and an instinct for living that may rely on hard work, but doesn’t depend on profiteering, as a reporter notices when Ed talks about his long life in citrus farming.
“My wife once told me I’ve never had a job,” he said, relishing a line he’s probably repeated before, one that happens to be true.
“I’ve had a 365-day-a-year hobby.”
